title: FizzBuzz with custom rules
summary: Order your conditions correctly to satisfy overlapping rules.
prompt: Write classify(n). Return 'FizzBuzz' when n is divisible by both 3 and 5, 'Fizz' when divisible by 3 only, 'Buzz' when divisible by 5 only, and the number itself (as a number) otherwise. Negative numbers and zero follow the same rules (0 is divisible by everything).
constraints: n is an integer between -1000 and 1000
Return the number, not a string, when no rule applies
hints: Check the 'both' case before the single cases, or the single cases will win first.
n % 15 === 0 is the same as divisible by 3 and 5.
Return n unchanged (a number) in the final case.
explanation: The only trap is ordering: testing divisibility by 15 first guarantees the combined case is not shadowed by the single checks. The remainder operator works for negatives and zero in the same way, so no special handling is needed.

title: Sum of multiples below a limit
summary: Loop with a stopping condition and avoid double counting.
prompt: Write sumMultiples(limit, factors). Return the sum of every positive integer below limit that is a multiple of at least one number in factors. Each qualifying integer is counted once even if it matches several factors. If factors is empty or limit is 1 or less, return 0.
constraints: factors contains positive integers
hints: Loop n from 1 up to (but not including) limit.
some() answers 'is n divisible by any factor?' in one expression.
Adding n once per loop iteration avoids double counting automatically.
explanation: Iterating candidates rather than multiples of each factor sidesteps the double-counting problem: each n is added at most once. The loop bound is strict (< limit) as the statement requires.

title: Validate a username
summary: Apply several rules with guard clauses and return the first failure.
prompt: Write validateUsername(name). Return null when the username is valid, otherwise return the first failing rule's message, checked in this order: 'Required' when name is not a string or is empty after trimming; 'Too short' when fewer than 3 characters; 'Too long' when more than 16 characters; 'Invalid characters' when it contains anything other than letters, digits, or underscores; 'Must start with a letter' when the first character is not a letter. Do not trim the name before the length or character checks, only for the 'Required' check.
constraints: Check rules in the exact order given
Letters are a–z and A–Z only
hints: typeof name !== 'string' handles non-strings before you call any string method.
A regular expression such as /^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$/ tests allowed characters.
Order matters: return as soon as a rule fails.
explanation: Each rule is a guard clause that returns immediately, so the function reads as a checklist. The type check comes first because calling trim on a non-string would throw.
complexity: O(n) time in the length of the name, O(1) space

title: Compose a greeting
summary: Build small functions and combine them.
prompt: Write three functions. capitalize(word) returns the word with its first character upper-cased and the rest unchanged (empty string stays empty). exclaim(text) appends '!'. greet(name) returns 'Hello, ' followed by capitalize(name) followed by '!' by using the other two functions. Then write compose(f, g) that returns a new function h where h(x) equals f(g(x)).

contract.signature: capitalize(word: string): string; exclaim(text: string): string; greet(name: string): string; compose(f, g): (x) => any

constraints: greet must call capitalize and exclaim rather than building the string from scratch
compose returns a function
hints: word[0] is undefined for an empty string; guard for that.
greet can be written as exclaim('Hello, ' + capitalize(name)).
compose returns (x) => f(g(x)); g runs first.
explanation: Small pure functions are easy to test alone and to combine. compose demonstrates returning a function: the inner arrow closes over f and g and applies g first, then f.
complexity: O(n) in the string length for capitalize; O(1) otherwise

title: Average of any number of arguments
summary: Use a rest parameter and a default value.
prompt: Write average(precision = 2, ...values). Return the arithmetic mean of values rounded to precision decimal places, as a number. If no values are given, return 0. Passing undefined as the first argument must use the default precision of 2.
constraints: Return a number, not a string
0 <= precision <= 6
hints: values is a real array, so reduce works.
Number(x.toFixed(p)) converts the rounded string back to a number.
Guard for values.length === 0 before dividing.
explanation: The default applies when the first argument is omitted or undefined, and the rest parameter gathers everything after it. toFixed produces a string, so the result is converted back to a number as the contract requires.

title: Make a multiplier (and a counter)
summary: Return configured functions that remember their settings.
prompt: Write makeMultiplier(factor) that returns a function multiplying its argument by factor. Then write makeCounter(start = 0) that returns an object with two methods: next() returns the current value and then increases it by 1, and reset() sets the value back to start. Counters created separately must not share state.

contract.signature: makeMultiplier(factor: number): (n: number) => number; makeCounter(start?: number): { next(): number; reset(): void }

constraints: Do not use global variables for the counter state

tests.label: counter sequence
tests.expression: (() => { const c = makeCounter(); return [c.next(), c.next(), c.next()]; })()

tests.label: counter reset
tests.expression: (() => { const c = makeCounter(5); c.next(); c.reset(); return c.next(); })()

hidden_tests.label: independent counters
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter(10); a.next(); a.next(); return [a.next(), b.next()]; })()

hidden_tests.label: independent multipliers
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { const d = makeMultiplier(2); const t = makeMultiplier(3); return [d(5), t(5)]; })()

hints: The returned function closes over factor.
Keep the counter's current value in a let inside makeCounter, not on the returned object, so it is private.
reset must restore the original start, so keep start unchanged.
explanation: Each call to makeCounter creates a new scope with its own current variable, which both methods close over. Nothing outside can touch it, which is the classic closure-based privacy pattern.

title: Count words with an object
summary: Use an object as a tally with bracket notation.
prompt: Write countWords(text). Split the text on any whitespace, ignore empty pieces, lower-case each word, strip leading and trailing punctuation from the set . , ! ? ; : and return a plain object mapping each word to how many times it appears. Return an empty object for empty or whitespace-only input.
constraints: Keys are lower-case words with surrounding punctuation removed
Use a plain object, not a Map

hidden_tests.label: word that is a prototype key

hints: text.trim().split(/\s+/) splits on runs of whitespace.
A regex like /^[.,!?;:]+|[.,!?;:]+$/g removes punctuation at the ends only.
Use (counts[word] ?? 0) + 1 — but beware inherited keys like 'constructor'; Object.hasOwn or a null-prototype object avoids surprises.
explanation: An object works as a tally when you read the current value with a fallback and write it back. Words such as 'constructor' collide with inherited properties on a normal object, so the solution tallies in a null-prototype object and spreads it into a plain object at the end.
complexity: O(n) time in the number of characters, O(k) space for k distinct words

title: Bank account object
summary: Methods that share state through this and survive being detached.
prompt: Write createAccount(owner, opening = 0) returning an object with: balance (a number), deposit(amount) which adds a positive amount and returns the new balance, withdraw(amount) which subtracts a positive amount that does not exceed the balance and returns the new balance, and statement() returning `${owner}: ${balance}`. deposit and withdraw must throw a RangeError for non-positive amounts and withdraw must throw a RangeError for insufficient funds. The methods must keep working when extracted from the object, for example const w = account.withdraw; w(10).

contract.signature: createAccount(owner: string, opening?: number): { balance: number; deposit(n): number; withdraw(n): number; statement(): string }

constraints: Throw RangeError for invalid amounts
Detached methods must still operate on the same account

tests.label: statement
tests.expression: (() => { const a = createAccount('Ann', 10); a.deposit(5); return a.statement(); })()

hidden_tests.label: detached method keeps state
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { const a = createAccount('Ann', 100); const w = a.withdraw; w(40); return a.balance; })()

hidden_tests.label: insufficient funds throws RangeError
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { try { createAccount('Ann', 10).withdraw(20); return 'no throw'; } catch (e) { return e.name; } })()

hidden_tests.label: non-positive deposit throws RangeError
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { try { createAccount('Ann').deposit(0); return 'no throw'; } catch (e) { return e.name; } })()

hidden_tests.label: balance property updates
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { const a = createAccount('Ann'); a.deposit(25); return a.balance; })()

hints: A detached call has no this, so either use arrow functions that close over a local variable, or bind each method.
Keep the balance in a closure variable and expose it through a getter, or update both.
Validate the amount before changing anything.
explanation: Because the methods are arrow functions closing over a private balance variable, they do not depend on this at all, so detaching them is safe. A getter exposes balance as a read-only property that always reflects the closure value.

title: Extract an address safely
summary: Nested destructuring with defaults and optional chaining on incomplete records.
prompt: Write formatAddress(user). user may be missing entirely or missing any nested part. Read user.profile.address.{line1, city, postcode, country}. Return a single string joining the non-empty parts of line1, city, postcode with ', ' followed by ' (' + country + ')' where country defaults to 'IN'. If no address parts are available at all, return 'No address'.
constraints: Must not throw for undefined input or missing nested objects
Empty strings count as missing

tests.label: full address
tests.expression: formatAddress({ profile: { address: { line1: '12 MG Road', city: 'Pune', postcode: '411001', country: 'IN' } } })

hidden_tests.label: empty strings ignored
hidden_tests.expression: formatAddress({ profile: { address: { line1: '', city: 'Mumbai', postcode: '', country: 'IN' } } })

hidden_tests.label: other country
hidden_tests.expression: formatAddress({ profile: { address: { line1: '1 Rue', city: 'Paris', country: 'FR' } } })

hints: const { line1 = '', city = '', postcode = '', country = 'IN' } = user?.profile?.address ?? {};
Collect the parts in an array and filter(Boolean) before joining.
Decide on 'No address' by checking whether the filtered parts array is empty.
explanation: Optional chaining walks the nested path without throwing, ?? supplies an empty object so destructuring never fails, and per-key defaults handle missing fields. Filtering out empty strings before joining handles partial records.

title: Queue simulation
summary: Apply push, shift, and splice and report what was removed.
prompt: Write processQueue(initial, operations). Start with a copy of initial (do not mutate it). Each operation is an array: ['enqueue', item] adds to the end; ['dequeue'] removes from the front; ['remove', item] removes the first occurrence of item if present. Return an object { queue, removed } where queue is the final array and removed lists every item that was removed by dequeue or remove, in order.

contract.signature: processQueue(initial: any[], operations: any[][]): { queue: any[]; removed: any[] }

constraints: initial must not be mutated
dequeue on an empty queue does nothing
hints: Start with const queue = [...initial].
shift() returns undefined on an empty array; only record it when the queue had items.
indexOf then splice(index, 1) removes one occurrence; splice returns the removed items.
explanation: Copying first protects the caller's array. Each operation maps to one mutating method, and the return values of shift and splice are what feed the removed list.
complexity: O(n × m) worst case for m operations on a queue of n items

title: Cart summary
summary: Chain filter, map, and reduce on an order list.
prompt: Write summarize(items). Each item is { name, price, qty, taxable }. Ignore items with qty of 0 or less. Return { count, subtotal, tax, total, names } where count is the number of items kept, subtotal is the sum of price × qty, tax is 18% of the subtotal of taxable items only, total is subtotal + tax, and names is an array of the kept item names in original order. Round subtotal, tax, and total to 2 decimals as numbers.

contract.signature: summarize(items: Array<{ name: string; price: number; qty: number; taxable: boolean }>): { count: number; subtotal: number; tax: number; total: number; names: string[] }

constraints: Do not mutate items
Round with 2 decimals; return numbers

tests.label: mixed cart
tests.expression: summarize([{ name: 'Tea', price: 40, qty: 2, taxable: true }, { name: 'Cake', price: 120, qty: 1, taxable: false }, { name: 'Water', price: 20, qty: 0, taxable: true }])

tests.label: single taxable item
tests.expression: summarize([{ name: 'Tea', price: 100, qty: 1, taxable: true }])

hidden_tests.label: all taxable
hidden_tests.expression: summarize([{ name: 'A', price: 10, qty: 1, taxable: true }, { name: 'B', price: 5, qty: 2, taxable: true }])

hidden_tests.label: rounding
hidden_tests.expression: summarize([{ name: 'A', price: 0.1, qty: 3, taxable: true }])

hidden_tests.label: negative qty ignored
hidden_tests.expression: summarize([{ name: 'A', price: 10, qty: -1, taxable: true }])

hidden_tests.label: input not mutated
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { const items = [{ name: 'A', price: 1, qty: 1, taxable: false }]; summarize(items); return items.length; })()

hints: Filter once into a kept array and reuse it for count, names, and totals.
Compute the taxable subtotal separately with another filter/reduce.
A helper round2 = (n) => Math.round(n * 100) / 100 keeps results numeric.
explanation: filter selects, map transforms, reduce combines. Computing the kept list once and deriving everything from it keeps the function readable, and rounding at the end avoids accumulating float error in the middle.

title: Top scores with tie-breaks
summary: A multi-key comparator that must not mutate the input.
prompt: Write topScores(players, n). players is an array of { name, score }. Return a new array of the top n players sorted by score descending, then by name ascending (case-insensitive) for equal scores. If n is larger than the number of players, return all of them. The input array must not be reordered.

contract.signature: topScores(players: Array<{ name: string; score: number }>, n: number): Array<{ name: string; score: number }>
contract.returns: new sorted array of length min(n, players.length)

constraints: Do not mutate players
Names compare case-insensitively

tests.label: top two
tests.expression: topScores([{ name: 'Bo', score: 80 }, { name: 'Al', score: 95 }, { name: 'Cy', score: 80 }], 2)

hidden_tests.label: input not reordered
hidden_tests.expression: (() => { const p = [{ name: 'b', score: 1 }, { name: 'a', score: 2 }]; topScores(p, 2); return p.map((x) => x.name); })()

hidden_tests.label: case-insensitive tie-break
hidden_tests.expression: topScores([{ name: 'bob', score: 5 }, { name: 'Amy', score: 5 }], 2).map((p) => p.name)

hidden_tests.label: three-way tie
hidden_tests.expression: topScores([{ name: 'c', score: 9 }, { name: 'a', score: 9 }, { name: 'b', score: 9 }], 3).map((p) => p.name)

hints: toSorted (or [...players].sort) keeps the original untouched.
b.score - a.score sorts descending; use || to fall through to the name comparison when it is 0.
a.name.localeCompare(b.name, undefined, { sensitivity: 'base' }) compares case-insensitively; slice(0, n) takes the top n.
explanation: The comparator returns the score difference first; when that is 0 the || operator falls through to the name comparison. Copying with spread before sort preserves the caller's order, and slice handles n beyond the length naturally.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Title case a sentence
summary: split, map, slice, and join working together.
prompt: Write titleCase(text). Return the text with the first letter of every word upper-cased and the remaining letters lower-cased. Words are separated by single spaces in the output regardless of how many spaces separated them in the input. Leading and trailing whitespace is removed. Empty input returns an empty string.
constraints: Collapse runs of whitespace to a single space
hints: trim() then split(/\s+/) gives clean words; an empty string needs a guard because ''.split gives [''].
word[0].toUpperCase() + word.slice(1).toLowerCase() handles each word.
join(' ') rebuilds the sentence.
explanation: The pipeline is split → map → join. Splitting on a whitespace regex normalises spacing for free, and the empty-string guard avoids calling toUpperCase on undefined.
